en: The Sūtra on the Girl Vimaladattā, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, together with...

He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand, all of whom were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained what was to be done, who were free from defilement and had attained mastery, who had laid down the heavy burden and achieved their own benefit, who had utterly removed all fetters of beginning and end, who had crossed over by means of wisdom and attained penetrating insight, and who were all virtuous and noble, like great dragons whose minds had attained sovereignty. Among them was the great man and worthy Ānanda;

and ten thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom had become great arhats—all of whom were holy and realized, whose supernormal powers were fully developed, and who were all non-retrogressive regarding the wheel of Dharma. The names of these bodhisattvas were:

The Bodhisattva Jewel Light, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Accumulation, the Bodhisattva Renowned Head, the Bodhisattva Eloquence Accumulation, the Bodhisattva Universal Head, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Worthy Head, the Bodhisattva Joyful King, the Bodhisattva Whose Practice Enters the Inconceivable Gate of Liberation, the Bodhisattva Who Mindfully Contemplates All Dharmas Without Obstruction, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Who Enters the Nature of Resolve, the Bodhisattva Who Abandons All Evil Realms, the Bodhisattva Who Dispels the Darkness of All Sorrows, the Bodhisattva Who Transcends Desire and Leaves No Trace of Falsity, the Bodhisattva Unfailing Vision, the Bodhisattva Adorned with Virtuous Jewels, the Bodhisattva Golden Jewel Radiant Head, the Bodhisattva Who Has Cast Off All Obscurations, and the Bodhisattva Harmless Mind—these and others, numbering ten thousand bodhisattvas in all, were fully present.

At that time, there were the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Revata, Aniruddha, Ānanda, and others; as well as the youth Mañjuśrī, Amoghadarśin, Ratnaketu, Sarvaduḥkhapramocaka, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Avalokiteśvara, Pratibhānakūṭa, and Vimalagati.

Then these eight bodhisattvas and their eight disciples, having dressed in their robes and taken up their alms bowls at dawn, entered the city to beg for food; as they walked together, they deliberated with one another and each made a vow.
Śāriputra said:
"One should enter the city for alms while abiding in such a samādhi as this, so that all people therein may universally hear the Four Noble Truths."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"May all the people within the city never, for even a moment, give rise to demonic activities that obstruct giving. Mahākāśyapa said:
“May all those within the city who bestow food upon me obtain inexhaustible merit that leads to the attainment of Nirvāṇa. Subhūti said:
“May all those within the city who behold this radiance, by virtue of this causal retribution, be reborn in the heavens or among humans, and thereafter attain the Dharma of Nirvāṇa.”
Pūrṇa said: "May all the heterodox practitioners, brahmins, and elders within that city attain right view. Revata said:
"May all the people within the city be free from calamity and sin, and may they all attain peace and security.
Aniruddha said, "May all the people within the city all obtain the divine eye."
Ānanda said, "I pray that all the people within the city may fully recognize and remember the sūtras and dharmas they have heard in the past. Mañjuśrī said:

He transformed the gates, windows, and doors within the city, as well as the multi-storied pavilions, vihāras, utensils, necklaces, trees with their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, and the ornaments of clothing, so that they all proclaimed the sounds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-attainment, non-arising, and non-ceasing; sounds of non-laxity, non-attachment, formlessness, lack of categories, and the absence of self (*anātman*).
Avitathadarśin said:

"All the men and women, great and small, within that city who see with their own eyes this transformation shall all behold the form of the Buddha; until the ultimate end, they shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
Ratnaketu said: "May all the treasuries belonging to every household within this city be filled with various jewels. Vikṣiptāpāya said:

He transformed all the people dwelling within the city, so that whoever dared to commit an offense deserving of hellish retribution would have their current offenses rendered slight and suddenly extinguished.
Jiezhuyingai said: "I transform the people within the city so that they cast off the five hindrances and do not allow them to increase. Guangshiyin said:
He transforms those within it such that those confined in prisons are set free, all captives are released from their bonds, and all who are terrified attain fearlessness.
Vetragupta said: "May those among the people there who dare to see us all attain eloquence, and may their various musical performances be transformed into conversational discourse.
Anābhogagati-vikrāmin said:
"May all those people whom we behold therein be led to the ultimate attainment of the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way.
At that time, the eight bodhisattvas and the eight great disciples, having each deliberated thus together, arrived at the city gate.

At that time, King Prasenajit in the city had a daughter named Vimaladattā (translated into Chinese as Lìgòushī, meaning "Stainless Bestowal"), who was twelve years of age. She was exceptionally beautiful and exquisite; all who saw her were filled with joy. She was the most pure and white, her complexion like a wondrous flower.

On the eighth day of the month, at the time of the morning star, he mounted his carriage at dawn with five hundred female attendants; five hundred brahmins followed behind him as he went out for a tour of inspection and proceeded to a sacrificial altar, intending to perform a great sacrifice.
At that time, when the brahmins saw the bhikṣus from afar, they thought in their hearts that it was an ill omen.
Among the brahmins was one who was advanced in years and decrepit, named Brahmā; he said to the girl Vimaladattā:
"You should know that today is inauspicious, for we see these bhikṣus stationed at the city gate."
"Stop! There is no need to go out; you should return to the city.
Upon seeing such people as these, whatever benefits or goals you seek will certainly not be realized as you wish."
Then the maiden Vimaladattā addressed the brahmin in verse, saying: “The resolve and conduct of these [monks],
and their merit in teaching and transforming others, are the most auspicious and peaceful among all sacrificial offerings.”
If a brahmin can make offerings to these [sages], all will be auspicious and there shall never be any difference.
Thus, through the Brahma-precepts, he becomes disciplined, concentrated, and serene; transcending all evils, he is free from the defilement of worldly dust.

These practices constitute the supreme and excellent physician; they provide consolation and treatment for the long-standing ailments of sentient beings. This is the stainless, foremost standard for teachers.
For the sake of countless people, you have removed all evil deeds; regarding the four views, you have become clearly enlightened.
O Brahmin, you have come at a most auspicious time; the Buddha dwells in the world, the most supreme Dharma King.
These are my sons, who have achieved the state of Arhat; now these Bodhisattvas are my most honored teachers.
What person of wisdom would abandon them and depart?
The Honored One among two-legged beings is the supreme field of merit; those who wish to be born in heaven should bestow these manifold blessings.
If one gives with such kindness, the retribution will be immeasurable, and wherever one dwells, there shall never be depletion.
Following these teachings, one becomes endowed with the marks and signs of excellence; such a person is a field of merit, pure in disposition and nature.
Even if a brahmin should give rise to a heart of joy, they shall thereby attain peace and security, departing from the mundane world.
Devotedly practicing the Way of the Buddhas, their resolve has never been disturbed; as they go on alms-round, they always observe with diligence.
Wherever they dwell or travel, they skillfully guard their sense faculties; with their faculties stilled and settled, this assembly is like the great ocean.
The waters of rivers and seas may still be measured in liters; the lands of the ten directions may likewise be traversed on foot.
But if there is one who practices giving—a king among men—his every deed is beyond all measure.
When the kalpa is consumed by fire, Mount Sumeru is destroyed, the rivers and seas dry up, and all the earth perishes;
yet for one who makes offerings to those honored as kings among men, though the kalpa be afflicted by calamity, their merit cannot be burned away.
Thereupon, the brahmin replied to Vimaladattā with these verses:
"Do not act according to your own whims, following a foolish and deluded mind.
Do not, at the time of sacrifice, take pleasure in the bhikṣu."
"These shaven-headed ones, clad in saffron robes—if your mind finds peace and liberation, you need not associate with this faction.
We fear that your parents will not be pleased; we shall therefore inform the Great Enlightened King."
"The offerings made by a woman are likewise inauspicious.
How excellent, O noble lady! Do not accept this bhikṣu.
Thereupon, Vimaladattā replied to the brahmin in verse:
"If one falls into the evil realms, amidst the hardships of birth and death, though one has parents, they cannot provide rescue or relief.
Nor can others, nor wealth, nor divine mantras; only those of this kind [the Buddhas] are able to deliver and liberate."
I cast off my body and scatter it in all directions; with reverence, joy, love, and respect, I take refuge in the Buddha.
From now until the end, I do not hope for the salvation of any other person, but shall rely solely upon the Triple Gem.
Just as one who has lost their sight gazes into a bright mirror,
so too are the non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners of no benefit;
the Brahmin is like Mount Sumeru on fire.
Having heard much in this way, liberation through effort is the essential;
never lacking in the wisdom of extensive learning, one becomes fully equipped with all that is to be heard.
"If one is able to hear this and immediately put it into practice, this constitutes true upholding; it is something that all others find difficult to reach.
Thereupon, the brahmin said to the girl Vimaladattā:
"I have never before seen such a venerable Buddha and assembly of bhikṣus; by what causes and conditions has such joy arisen in you?"
The woman then replied:
"Brahmin! Do you wish to know?"
When I was first born, my mother placed me upon a bed of gold and jewels; at that moment, five hundred devaputras were flying together through the void above, and I beheld them.
They extolled the merits of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha with countless praises, and I heard their voices.
At that time, there was a son of heaven within the assembly who had never before seen the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One. He asked the other sons of heaven:
"Regarding the Tathāgata whom you all praise, what are his virtues like?"
At that time, the sons of the gods, perceiving my thoughts and seeing that my mind was filled with profound faith, immediately spoke this verse in praise of the Buddha:
“Your hair is a deep azure-blue, Pure, beautiful, and curling to the right,
Like a hundred-petaled lotus in water;”
Like the full moon in its brilliant radiance;
the white hair between his brows curls like the light of snow;
his superior eyes are like blue lotuses, like the king of bees.
The Honored Teacher among Men is like a lion; his lips are like vermilion, and his eyebrows and eyelashes are exceedingly fine and exquisite, even, straight, and most beautiful.
His broad and long tongue covers his face, reaching all the way to the hairline.
His teaching is pure, harmonious, and pleasing, satisfying the minds of the wise.
His voice is like bells and drums, lutes, flutes, and pipes;
its tone is both harmonious and elegant, just like the sounds of the *qin*, *se*, and *zheng* zithers.
The sorrowful luan-bird and the kiṃnara sing in the forest; yet the most supreme voice transcends them all.
His words are like the lion’s roar; his wondrous sound destroys all maladies.
Having already abandoned all defilements, his speech is truthful and severs all views;
whether walking or sitting among the assembly, those who hear him find all their doubts resolved.
His words are without flaw or omission, bringing joy to all people.
Surpassing himself, he has abandoned both extremes, just like the attainment of nirvāṇa.
His speech is free from arrogance or indulgence, and his physical form is most wondrous.
His words are plain and without flattery or ornamentation; all these are for the sake of teaching and practicing for the multitude.
Like a garland woven from gathered flowers, such is the Buddha’s melodic wisdom.
All his mindfulness is perfectly fulfilled; his noble arms extend beyond his knees, his palms are even and symmetrical, and his fingers are slender, long, and beautiful.
Majestic and firm is his body; his precious countenance is like purple-gold.
The Buddha’s form shines like the sun, appearing from afar while his voice is heard everywhere.
His hair is soft and deep blue, with each strand curling to the right.
His thighs are like those of a dragon or elephant, and his knees are broad and well-proportioned.
His feet are level and even as if painted, with the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel (*cakra*) arising from below;
such are the virtues of the Buddha.
Having no longing for the world, he has crossed over all realms of existence;
the Great Compassionate and Supreme Physician, his primary task is to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
He severs all fetters and is unattached, like a lotus flower.
“O Brahmin, I have heard from the devas such praise of the Buddha as this.
The girl Vimaladattā said to the Brahmin:
“Since I have heard such praise of the Buddha’s merits from the various devas, I have not been conscious of sleep since then, nor have I had any thoughts of lust, anger, delusion, or harmful intent.”

From that time forth, he has not been conscious of or attached to his parents, brothers, sisters, relatives, or acquaintances; nor has he cherished necklaces, garments, his own body, or his life, nor has he sought pleasure in cities or excursions.
He has focused solely on reverent devotion, mindfulness of the Buddha, the Great Sage.
Brahmin! You should know that for this reason, wherever the Tathāgata extensively expounds the Dharma, I listen to it all, never missing a single word or its profound and wondrous meaning.
I constantly observe and behold the Buddha day and night, never failing to see him.
Because I behold the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, throughout the day and night, I desire to hear the Dharma and to pay respectful homage to the Noble Assembly, never feeling weary or satiated.
At that time, Vimaladattā praised the virtues of the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones.
When the Brahmā, the brahmin, and the multitude of five hundred people heard this, they were filled with joy and all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

The woman immediately descended from her carriage and approached the bodhisattvas and great disciples; she bowed her head to them all, prostrating at the feet of each one with single-minded reverence, and stood with her palms joined.
At that time, Śāriputra gazed upon the girl Vimaladattā.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Śāriputra:
"O Virtuous One!..."

For those with female bodies who dwell within the two consciousnesses, sensual desires are like fire; they are full of negligence, delighting in what is pleasing while their minds do not follow right mindfulness, nor do they aspire toward liberation, but instead indulge themselves in heedlessness.
"Excellent, worthy one!
Please preach the Dharma to us as is appropriate; out of compassion, grant us peace and security for the long night, free from all difficulties.
Just as these words were being finished, King Prasenajit, together with his various ministers, arrived at that place.
Upon hearing these words, the king said to the girl Vimaladattā,
"You who delight in renunciation, for what reason do you exert yourself so diligently, with such a haggard countenance, as you wander here?"
"Since birth I have never walked on foot, nor have I ever slept; now that I have finally resolved to practice, I find no pleasure in it and have nothing with which to amuse myself.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit spoke these verses for Vimaladattā:
"With features so pure and exquisite, Like a celestial jade maiden, Adorned with necklaces and ornaments,"
Your garments are perfumed with incense;
as for this female body you now possess, what is there to be weary of or loathe?
Since you are free from the sloth of sleep, you dwell within the kingdom.
The storehouses are overflowing with wealth;
the woman’s parents always enjoy freedom—what could they not find joyful? Now she has attained self-mastery.
For what reason does her heart not take pleasure in the life of a householder?
Furthermore, she is pleasing to the eyes of her parents and is revered by all people.
Why do you not take pleasure in wandering and sitting here?
You have adorned your body with various necklaces; have you not heard of this, or have you seen it?
For this reason, I am filled with dread and my heart is weary.
Daughter, you ought to declare this intention for me.
As for your current vow, what wish do you seek to fulfill?
Then Vigatamala-dānā spoke these verses to her father, the king:
"Great King, you do not perceive the peril of birth and death, nor the affliction of the aggregates (*skandha*).
This body is fragile and precarious; it is driven by thoughts of craving and desire, and its actions are like a magical illusion."
Human life in this world does not endure for even a moment.
Great Father, you should realize that I am dwelling among poisonous snakes; how could I find sleep or indulge in any desires?
Reflecting upon this now, the four venomous snakes thought to themselves:
"What joy can there be?
Being oppressed by our enemies and dwelling in manifold sufferings, how can we find peace?"
The enemy of worldly toil appears so abruptly; how can I find delight in pleasures?
For one who has fallen into poison, who can sleep?
"Without having abandoned one's enemies, how can there be joy?
Having fallen into a great pit and trench, what can one rely upon?
O Great King, you should know that dwelling in the world is thus."
Now, observing that you are most supreme and sovereign, I have immediately resolved my mind to attain Buddhahood.
O King, listen to my words:
"I have never seen or heard of one who, having become a bodhisattva, harbors negligence."
Fearing predatory beasts, they flee in all directions;
enemies brandishing staves and raising blades pursue them;
moreover, overcome by hunger and thirst, they enter an empty village.
Fearing the thieves of birth and death, who could find joy in this?
"This painted chest that is the body—consider it to be just like this:
though one constantly harbors it, it is inhabited by the four beasts and the four venomous snakes."
“Infinite are the hindrances and obscurations, the perils of hostile thieves;
who would find joy in the wilderness, that realm of fear?
Thereupon, Vimaladattā said to Śāriputra:
"Ask only, worthy one! You should answer me concerning the matter of wisdom.
As for what is called wisdom, it is praised by the elders as the most venerable."
Is that wisdom conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? If it were conditioned,
it would be a phenomenon subject to arising, ceasing, and destruction— a deceptive and false dharma.
That which is unconditioned is free from the three marks; for this reason, it is without arising.
That which is without arising is without conjunction.
"As for that wisdom, it is entirely non-existent.
At that time, Śāriputra remained silent and had no reply.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"Virtuous Śāriputra! At that time, you were the one who sent forth Vimaladattā with her questions. Śāriputra replied:
“The awakening of a woman does not concern the conditioned or the unconditioned; it is the teaching of non-arising, which cannot be answered or dispatched by means of vocal sounds.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

“The World-Honored One has praised you, O Worthy One, as the foremost in supernormal powers among the elders. How is it, do you manifest supernormal powers while maintaining the notion of a multitude of people?”
Is it by means of the notion of a phenomenon (*dharma-saṃjñā*)?

If one were to manifest supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*) by establishing the notion of a person (*pudgala-saṃjñā*), then since the person is empty and lacks reality, the supernormal powers would likewise be void.
If you wish to do so by means of the notion of a phenomenon, phenomena are devoid of any creative agency (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).
"Where there is nothing created, there is nothing obtained.
Because there is nothing obtained, there is no conceptualization.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana remained silent and offered no reply.
Mahākāśyapa said: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Dispatch the woman’s question at this time."
Maudgalyāyana replied:

"The question asked by this woman is not based on conceptual thought; it is beyond the discourse of ideation, being without fabrication and without recollection. Only the Tathāgatas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas are able to provide an answer."
The girl Vimaladattā asked Mahākāśyapa:
"The Buddha has praised you, Elder, as foremost among those who are content with little;
how is it, Kāśyapa, that while dwelling in the eight inconceivable gates of dhyāna-samādhi, you still compassionately wander for alms out of pity for all beings?"
Regarding those who receive food— such as one who offers a single ladle to such a person— they shall all be reborn in heaven.
Is this because they have completed their bodily service for the sake of the multitude of blessings, or is it because they have understood with their minds?
If one were to employ the body, the body belongs to the external; thus, one cannot settle the matter by means of the body!
To conceive of the body as such is like regarding grass, trees, walls, tiles, or stones; for this reason, it cannot be used to discern or resolve the matter.
If one applies the mind, the mind has no place of abiding, and for that reason it does not understand.
If one posits that body and mind exist externally, then they are non-existent and cannot be understood.
Kāśyapa remained silent. Subhūti said: "O Mahākāśyapa!
"At that time, it was the woman who sent forth the question. Kāśyapa replied:
"If what the woman has now asked is entirely without anything received, then it accords with the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi)."
"For this reason, she cannot be sent away. The girl Vimaladattā asked Subhūti:
"The Buddha has praised you, Elder, as being foremost among those who dwell in seclusion and practice emptiness."
Regarding this teaching of emptiness, is there anything that can be spoken of, or is it merely praising the existence of form?
If one wishes to speak of the Dharma, the Dharma has neither the characteristic of arising nor the characteristic of ceasing.
That which possesses the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing is equanimity.

That which is equanimous is disciplined composure. That which is disciplined composure is rootless. That which is rootless is also without action. That which is without action is beyond verbal expression. That which is beyond verbal expression is without mental ideation. That which is without mental ideation is without reality.
"If there is nothing that exists, then there is no reality; that which lacks reality is what the sages and worthies praise.
Subhūti remained silent, having no further words with which to respond.
Pūrṇa said: "Subhūti,
you should now provide an answer to the question posed by this woman."
Subhūti said: "One should not say anything regarding this;
silence is peace."
Why is this so? The question posed by you, daughter, concerns no matter of heedlessness.
To speak of it otherwise would be to fall into deficiency and to conceive of a dharma-realm as something finite.
"Where there is no verbal expression, one returns to emptiness.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Pūrṇa:
"The Buddha praised the worthy one, saying that your exposition of the Dharma is most supreme."
For what reason and by what causal conditions does the Elder preach the Dharma?
If he were without causes and conditions, there would be no benefit.
If he were to expound the Dharma by means of causes and conditions, he would be equal to ignorant, ordinary worldlings.
Why is this? Because foolish worldlings are conjoined with causes and conditions; therefore, the worthy one does not depart from the dharmas of foolish worldlings.
If there were no causes and conditions, there would be no forms or categories; how then could one speak of the Dharma?
"Because there is no object for it to confront. Pūrṇa remained silent. Revata said:
“Worthy one! Please answer the question posed by the woman at this opportune time. Pūrṇa replied:
"What you have now asked does not employ conventional inquiry to reach ultimate liberation; as for ultimate liberation, it is a realm beyond words and cannot be described.
The maiden Vimaladattā then asked Revata:
"The Buddha praised you, Elder, saying that your practice of dhyāna is most supreme."
By what mind does one rely upon and abide in dhyāna?
Is it by means of no mind?
If one were to employ a mind, that mind would be like an illusion—empty and non-existent—and thus the samādhi of meditative concentration would likewise be non-existent.
Even if one were without mind, all waters, dwellings, palaces, houses, grasses, trees, branches, and leaves would all attain samādhi.
Why is this? Because these things are without mind.
Revata remained silent. Anuruddha said,
"Venerable friend!
"Please dismiss her at the proper time and inquire after her. Revata replied,
"As for what this woman has discussed— questioning the realm of the Buddha— that is not something a disciple can resolve."
The woman asked Revata:
"How is it, worthy one? Is the Dharma of the śrāvakas different from that of the Tathāgata?"
If one were to establish distinctions, then that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would necessarily be differentiated; yet all noble ones (*ārya*) are entirely unconditioned!
That which is unconditioned has no arising; that which has no arising has no duality; and that which is non-dual cannot be named as two.
"Why did you say this? Śānta was unable to reply.
The girl Vimaladattā then asked Aniruddha:
“The Buddha has praised you, Venerable One, as having the most honored divine eye. How is it, worthy one!
Do you see anything by means of that divine eye?”
Is it that there is no seeing?
If there were something seen, it would constitute permanence; if there were nothing seen, one would fall into nihilism.
Since what is seen has no form, does it have distinctions?
Anuruddha remained silent.
Ānanda said: "Venerable friend!"
"Dispatch her at once to ask her questions.
Anuruddha replied, "As for the questions she asks, except for one of fierce wisdom, they cannot be answered with words; silence is the way to bring peace."
The girl Vimaladattā asked Ānanda:
"The Buddha praised the Venerable One as the most eminent in extensive learning.
Now, what does it mean for you, O Benevolent One, to be so extensively learned?"
To what does "meaning" (artha) tend?
Is it for the purpose of adornment?
If it is by means of meaning, then meaning is beyond verbal expression.

That which is beyond verbal expression cannot be discriminated by the auditory consciousness; since the ear has nothing to cognize and thus cannot discriminate, that which cannot be discriminated is without words.
To rely on external adornments is contrary to what the World-Honored One has said:
"One should take refuge in the true meaning; do not grasp at adornments.
Therefore, the worthy do not consider extensive learning to be essential.
Ānanda remained silent. Mañjuśrī said, "Venerable Ānanda!
"Please answer at this time the questions posed by this woman. Ānanda replied:

"The questions this woman has asked now transcend the explanation of written words; they cannot be resolved through mere erudition. She asks about the essential meaning, yet the essential meaning is mindless. Being mindless, it has no location; it is not a principle that can be articulated by scholars, but belongs only to the Dharma King and those who have attained the Perfections."
The girl Vimaladattā asked Mañjuśrī, “The Buddha has praised you,
saying that among all bodhisattvas, you are the most supreme in terms of your profound and subtle faith and understanding.”
Is it deep because the twelve links of dependent origination are deep?
Or is it deep because its nature is naturally deep?
If one considers dependent origination to be profound and subtle, yet that very dependent origination has no place of operation.

Why is this so? That which is dependent origination neither comes nor goes; it cannot be specifically known as that which is cognized by the eye, nor can it be specifically known as that which is reached by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mental consciousness. Dependent origination alone is without any habitual activity.
"If that which is profound by virtue of being spontaneous were itself spontaneous, then that spontaneity would lack any spontaneity; even one who realizes spontaneity would have nothing to realize.
Mañjuśrī replied, "Because the primordial limit (*koṭi*) is profoundly subtle, it is called 'profound.'"
The girl replied:
“Because the original limit is itself limitless, for this reason, those two types of wisdom are non-existent wisdom. Mañjuśrī said:
"If there is no wisdom, then there is perversion; its ultimate limit is merely a conventional designation.
The daughter replied, "That which is without wisdom is also without perversion—this is what is meant."
"Even that which transcends verbal expression cannot be apprehended, yet it is without inversion. Mañjuśrī said,
"I have spoken this merely by means of provisional words."
The girl replied, "The Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva transcend all verbal expression; they cannot be fully articulated through words.
Then, the girl Vimaladattā questioned Abhīru-darśana:
He spoke thus to the son of good family:

"May all the people within the city attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and may all men and women, great and small, who behold this radiance with their own eyes, perceive the Tathāgata’s ultimate, perfect enlightenment."
"How is it? Does the Tathāgata possess a physical body (rūpakāya), or is he the Dharma-body (dharmakāya)?
If he were the Dharma-body, then he would have no form or image; if one were to see him as having a physical body, then one would not be seeing the Buddha."
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who see me by my form, or seek to hear me by my voice, harbor deluded and false views; such people do not see the Buddha."
"Furthermore, even by means of the Dharma-body, the Dharma-body cannot be seen. Why is this?
Because that which is the Dharma-body has relinquished visual consciousness; being without any conditioned activity, the affairs of worldly convention cannot be perceived therein."
Avivāhita remained silent. Ratnaketu said,
"Please answer the question posed by this maiden at this time."
Avitathadarśin said, "The woman asks about that which has no category; it cannot be explained away.
The woman replied to Avitathadarśin:
“I do not ask about categories, nor do I ask about the absence of categories.
At that time, Akṣayamati remained silent and had no response to these words.
The girl Vimaladattā then asked Ratnaśrī:
"Just now, that son of good family said:
'May all the ancient treasuries within this city manifest spontaneously, filled with various jewels.
Since you are such a person, will you bring those jewels here?"
For what purpose does one arrive at this view?

The Dharma has no need for clothing or food; were one to rely upon clothing and food, one would be identical to the deluded worldlings, for it is precisely because they are deluded worldlings that they constantly rely upon clothing and food.
"Even if one lacks clothing and food, one does not rely upon any of the various treasures found in the world.
Jewel-Flower remained silent.
The girl Vimaladattā then asked Abandoner-of-all-Evil-Destinations:
"Address the son of good family with these words:

'May all the people within this city who have committed offenses deserving of hell find that their misfortunes and transgressions in this present life become slight and minor; may they cast off all evils beyond measure.'"
As the Buddha has said:
"Whatever transgressions a person commits, they must inevitably undergo their consequences; escape from them is impossible.
If escape is impossible, how can one wish for the ignorant to have their offenses rendered minor?
"All phenomena are without a master; one wishes to make them have a master.
One has actions of one's own; one wishes to make them non-action.
Thus he spoke, casting aside all evil destinies.
"One should cause one's offenses to become slight through the power of vows. The woman replied:
"Furthermore, son of good family!"
All dharmas are equal and cannot be moved or altered by vows.
Even if one were capable, should each and every person give rise to a vow and think in their own mind:
"I shall deliver all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa."
"If what you have vowed can indeed be accomplished, then you ought to be able to control it so that your vow does not regress.
Having cast off all evil destinies, he remained silent and gave no verbal reply.
The girl Vimaladattā asked the bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
"Just now, noble son, you gave rise to this thought:
'May all the people in the city be freed from the bonds of the afflictions and various fetters, and rid themselves of the five hindrances.'"
"Regarding this samādhi of yours that can stabilize the mind, you wish to ensure that people do not increase the five hindrances.
What do you think?
Does this samādhi belong to yourself or to others?"
If all dharmas were to belong to oneself, they would all be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and devoid of conjunction.
How then, O virtuous one, can you, through samādhi-concentration, cause all people not to be attached to the five hindrances?
"Even if one were to entrust them to another, one could not thereby create a debt of gratitude for that other person.
Abandoning all hindrances (*nīvarana*), he said:
"One should treat this with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)."
The girl replied, “All Buddhas practice a mind of loving-kindness; yet there are Buddha-lands where all sentient beings remain perpetually inexhaustible.”
Having cast off all hindrances and obscurations, he remained silent and spoke no word.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Avalokiteśvara:
"Just now, that son of good family uttered these words:"
"May all the people dwelling within the city who are confined in prisons be set free; may all those held in captivity naturally escape their bonds, and may all who are in fear attain fearlessness."
"Does that which is being treated receive the aggregates (skandhas) or not?
If it were to receive them, it would belong to the foolish; therefore, it cannot be that there is no receiving of the aggregates."
"If there is nothing received, then there is nothing to be done; that which is not to be done cannot be accomplished.
Avalokiteśvara remained silent. Bianji said:
“Answer the questions posed by the woman at the appropriate time. Avalokiteśvara said:
“The questions posed by the woman neither arise nor cease; for this reason, they cannot be answered.”
The woman replied again:
"Regarding what was said by Avalokiteśvara, how could there be any question as to why [phenomena] neither arise nor cease?"
He replied, “Neither arising nor ceasing— there is no scriptural statement regarding that.
The woman then responded:

"To speak without words is the mark of a wise person; yet, by manifesting words, one provides instruction. Not being attached to words, one remains free from all obstructions; being free from obstructions is the Dharma-realm."
"For this reason, one who thoroughly understands the Dharma has nothing to which they are attached.
The girl Vimaladattā asked Prajñākūṭa:
"Noble son, you have just said these words:"
"May all the people within the city who behold me with their own eyes, as well as those whom I see, all attain eloquence, so that the various musical instruments may converse with one another."
"Your eloquence, O Benevolent One, is as lofty as this!
By what kind of mindfulness is it established?
Does it arise from being established within this very state?"
If it were established by means of the arising of thought, then all sentient beings would likewise establish such thoughts;
for this reason, one does not attain tranquility.
If that which is produced were to achieve accomplishment, then it would be false!
"If one does not give rise to thought, then there is nothing to be done; where there is nothing to be done, there is neither tranquility nor lack of composure.
Bianji replied, "What I have aspired to is for the sake of those who have first resolved their minds to attain enlightenment; it is for them that I have manifested this aspiration."
"If anyone comes to see me, they shall all attain eloquence.
The woman replied again: "Noble son!"
Does that initial generation of the mind have a place of activity?
If it were to exist, it would constitute the view of eternalism; if it were non-existent, one could not call it a guide or leader.
“[He] is completely free from all conditioned activities. Bianji remained silent.
Then the girl Liugushi asked Chaodu Wuxuji:
He addressed the son of good family, saying to himself:
"May all the people within this city—whomever I have beheld or who dares to observe me—see me as not false, until they reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
"How is it that the Buddha-way is either existent or non-existent?
If it were existent, it would be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thus capable of being craved and grasped.
If it were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it would lack substantiality and truth, and could not be received or maintained."
Chaudu Wuxuji said, "That which is called the Way is a term for sagely wisdom.
The woman replied again:
"Does that noble wisdom have anything that arises?
And yet, does it perform the practice of quiescence?
If there were any arising, it would be a conceptualization of non-conformity, and one would thereby achieve conditioned wisdom!"
If one practices conditioned wisdom, one will become subject to the discriminations of ignorant and darkened consciousness.
If, however, one abides in tranquility, there will be no inversion, and thus no recurrence.
Because there is no returning [to conceptualization], the Bodhisattva, the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata, the Arhat, are without thought-conception.
Only the foolish and ignorant conceive of a "path"; they are not called wise ones.
Having transcended all things, he left no trace and remained silent without a word.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the great disciples and the bodhisattvas:
"Let us return from here; there is no need to enter the city to go on almsround again."
Why is this? This is the proper time for alms-gathering and the offering of food and provisions.
Since the daughter Vimaladattā preached the Dharma to us just now and we have listened and received it, today we shall take the Dharma as our nourishment.
Then the woman replied:
"O Subhūti! As for what you have just said, there is neither raising nor lowering."
"Virtuous one, how can you have any aspirations or harbor thoughts of wishing to go to a vihāra to dwell and reside there? O Subhūti!"
The conduct of a śramaṇa is to depart from his dwelling place without negligence and not to delight in self-indulgence.

The dharma of a śramaṇa is to be without attachment; being without attachment, one is without resentment. One who harbors no resentment has nothing further to practice; that which is "having nothing further to practice" is what is called the state of the noble sages.

The eight great disciples and eight bodhisattvas, five hundred brahmacārins, the maiden Vimaladattā, King Prasenajit, and the rest of the great assembly went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit before him.
The maiden Vimaladattā circumambulated the Buddha seven times, stood before the World-Honored One, and questioned him with verses:
"I question the World-Honored One, Who is peerless and difficult to equal,
Pure and without dependence, Whose fame is immeasurable."
"Saving and succoring sentient beings, he bestows the joy of ambrosia, asking:
'How does one become a bodhisattva and bring his practice to fulfillment?
Thereupon, Vimaladatta knelt with palms joined and questioned the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva subduing the hosts of Māra while beneath the tree?
What is meant by a bodhisattva shaking all the buddha-fields?
What is meant by a bodhisattva emitting light that universally illumines immeasurable buddha-lands?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the dharma of dhāraṇī from all buddhas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva achieving samādhi through a tranquil and concentrated mind?
What is meant by a bodhisattva perfecting all practices and obtaining the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda)?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who is always handsome?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who attains birth by transformation?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who is immensely wealthy and possesses abundant riches?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining great wisdom?
What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly knowing past lives?
What is meant by a bodhisattva meeting with all the Buddhas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the thirty-two marks?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to accomplish the eighty secondary characteristics?
What is meant by a bodhisattva obtaining eloquence?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the field of merit?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s retinue being always harmonious?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s aspiration for a buddha-field being fulfilled immediately as intended?
The Buddha said to the daughter Vimaladattā: "Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to pose such a question regarding this meaning is for the benefit of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it brings great peace and security, and is born of great compassion and pity. Listen attentively, listen attentively, O devas and people of the ten directions!"
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall explain it for you.
"Certainly, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
Vimaladattā and the assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha addressed Vimaladattā:
"Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they subdue the hosts of Māra beneath the tree.
What are these four? They never become greedily attached to the gains and offerings of others;..."
His resolve was always to take no pleasure in flowery or ornate speech;
he exhorted countless people to accord with their fundamental virtue;
and he directed unexcelled compassion toward all sentient beings.
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Never harboring jealousy, / Free from ornate adornment and beauty,"
Exhorting and transforming countless people, Causing them to practice the roots of all virtues;
Constantly observing and cultivating a compassionate heart Toward the people of the ten directions,
He subdues demonic adversaries And dwells wherever he travels with sovereign ease.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva causes all buddha-fields to tremble. What are these four?
Their words and deeds correspond with one another;
they enter into the profound patience of the Dharma;
and their aspiration for the virtuous and true Dharma is firm and steadfast.
To exhort and transform immeasurable multitudes of people, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and enabling them to joyfully cherish subtle and wondrous wisdom.
This is the fourth.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Speech and action are always in accord; One clearly understands the profound and subtle meaning.
One's vows are ever firm and steadfast; One attains the pure and white Dharma."
He exhorted and transformed countless people, causing them to set their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
By virtue of these four dharmas, he was able to shake billions of Buddha-lands.
The Buddha said to Vigatamala-dānā:
“Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they emit light that universally illumines immeasurable Buddha-lands. What are these four?
They are: constantly lighting lamps in dark places;”
In the final age of chaos, they shall also protect the scriptures;
for those who are disordered and unacquainted with the various teachings, they shall expound the Way of the sutras to manifest the light of the Dharma;
and they shall offer precious incense and flowers, scattering them before Buddhist temples.
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"One should constantly give lamps, the pure radiance,"
In the final age of darkness, one shall protect the scriptures and preach the Dharma for the sake of those who are heedless,
and offer rare and precious jewels as offerings to the stupas and monasteries.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva emits and radiates his light,
illuminating countless billions of Buddha-lands.
All people who receive this brilliance are led to ultimate great peace.
"Then one immediately resolves to seek the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Vigatamala-dānā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, through the service of all Buddhas, attains this dharma."
What are these four? They are:
giving various kinds of diverse and extraordinary gifts;
and bestowing all manner of necklaces, ornaments, and jade-like women upon those who seek them.
Day and night, he earnestly extols and proclaims the virtues of the Tathāgata;
having engaged in such practice, his resolve is largely directed toward the Prajñāpāramitā.
These are the four.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"By means of manifold generosity, One attains the dhāraṇīs;
Adorned with necklaces, One gives exquisite jade maidens."
Constantly extolling the virtues of the Buddha, Diligently and earnestly applying oneself to cultivation,
Seeking the Perfection of Wisdom, The sublime sagely wisdom of all Buddhas—
By virtue of this meritorious retribution, One attains the dhāraṇī.
Yet they practice with diligent vigor, not sitting for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Regarding all the teachings expounded by the Buddhas of the ten directions,
these men of powerful memory and penetration receive them all entirely.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, with a tranquil and concentrated mind, accomplishes samādhi.
What are these four?"
They feel weary of and loathe all conditioned activities within birth and death;
they take no pleasure in the household life and their resolve is always to renounce it;
they practice with diligence and cast aside worldly affairs.
"What one undertakes to establish and exalt as a grand enterprise—
this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having abandoned all places of worldly involvement, he cultivates a single-mindedness like space;
with a resolve free from negligence, he practices with diligence and is able to bring his cultivated tasks to ultimate completion."
When the mind attains these four virtuous practices, one follows and cultivates this tranquil and wondrous Buddha-way;
thereby, one attains samādhi with a serene mind and achieves the practice of the path to perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva brings all practices to completion and attains the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*). What are these four?
Constantly maintaining a light and agile body;
the mind never becoming indolent or negligent;
and remaining without attachment to any phenomena.
"To examine the four great elements as being like the realm of empty space—
this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Always keeping the body light and agile, with a mind that is gentle and free from indolence,
one never becomes attached to any phenomena;
single-mindedly establishing one's resolve, one observes the four great elements."
Yet always with equanimity, one gazes upon them as if they were empty space.
Regarding these four dharmas, by what cause can they be brought forth?
Through such wisdom and penetration, one attains immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
"Then, in a mere moment, they reach hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields,
behold countless Buddhas, and prostrate themselves before them in worship.
The Buddha said to Vimaladattā:
“Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they are always upright and handsome. What are these four?
They are never subject to anger; they are free from the fetters of contention, strife, and defilement.”
One prostrates with joyful devotion before Buddha-stūpas and monasteries;
one is earnest in adorning and establishing the prohibitions and precepts; one responds to others with kind words without obstruction;
and one regards the Dharma Master as if serving the World-Honored One himself.
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Do not harbor anger toward others; Abandon loathing and filth, and cleanse away all defilements."
Always maintain a most excellent mind focused on the Way; one should sweep Buddhist temples with reverence,
uphold the prohibitions of the Dharma and guard all the precepts, respond to others with kind words,
and as a bodhisattva, harbor no resentment, regarding the Dharma Master as the World-Honored One.
Because he is able to practice this sublime Dharma, the Bodhisattva’s mind is joyful and his resolve is courageous;
because of this, those who behold him find delight, and hundreds of countless people gaze upon him together.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains birth through transformation. What are these four?"
One should fashion images of the Buddha seated upon lotus flowers;

furthermore, one should grind blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses into powder as fine as dust, carrying it in full measure as an offering to the Tathāgata, or scattering it over stupas and monasteries;
one should feel deep compassion for all people and firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts.
"Never seeking out the faults or deficiencies of others—
this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
If one fashions an image of the Buddha seated upon a lotus, Grinds various flowers finely, and provides them all to a monastery;
If one seeks not the faults of others but cherishes compassion, Then one shall attain rebirth by transformation within a lotus.
Mindfully perceiving all beings throughout the ten directions, they encourage them toward all virtues so that they may attain liberation;
if one can practice these virtues and accord with such conduct, one will be born by transformation before the Honored Guide.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva becomes immensely wealthy and possesses abundant riches. What are these four?"
They constantly practice respectful giving without arrogance or indulgence;
they bestow fine garments upon others as gifts;
and they always maintain sincere faith, delighting in purity and goodness.
Setting aside wrong views,
these constitute the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If that person practices giving, with reverence and without arrogance or indulgence,
never having attachment toward any objects,
and being able to faithfully delight in the instructions of all Buddhas,"
One can thus always attain mastery and achieve great wealth and abundance.
With a mind focused on reverence and respect, free from flattery and envy,
never seeking out the faults of others, and devoid of any harsh or violent conduct.
"Her disposition was always simple and honest, and what she saw was upright and correct;
because she practiced in this way, she was always wealthy and possessed many treasures.
The Buddha told Vigatamala-dānā:
“Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they attain great wisdom. What are these four?
They never cherish or begrudge the sūtras;”
If there is any hesitation, they immediately resolve the doubt;
if they are practitioners, they discern things as they should be, and whatever they teach clarifies the reality of emptiness;
their bodies conform to all modes of conduct.
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"One who does not cherish the Dharma for their own sake, Is able to resolve the doubts of the multitude."
Constantly using teaching and exhortation to instruct others, they contemplate the principle of emptiness and the practices of the Buddhas.
If there are noble beings who practice this Dharma, they shall attain great wisdom and universal renown;
all are able to follow the teachings of the Buddhas and return to achieve these words of tranquil penetration.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva constantly remembers past lives.
What are these four?"
Reciting the sutras and constantly practicing with diligence, one masters what has long been forgotten; by reflecting on the old, one attains the new.
Regarding that which is to be recited, one discerns and explains the meaning of the phrases and sentences; with mind and mouth in accord, one lectures for others using gentle words.
Establishing immeasurable practices, one zealously cultivates and provides the gift of the Dharma.

Constantly protecting those suffering amidst the myriad afflictions of birth and death, he extols nirvana and proclaims peace and security; through skillful means, he thoroughly understands and adheres to the practice of samādhi, joyfully encouraging and assisting others.
"These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Reciting the scriptures to recall what has been forgotten, And explaining emptiness with a joyful mind."
One practices the sutras without ever growing weary, Single-mindedly contemplating samādhi, free from manifold thoughts.
By being able to practice these four dharmas, One comes to know past lives, vast and sublime;
With awareness spanning inconceivable thousands of kalpas, One swiftly attains Buddhahood as a guide for the multitude.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva meets with all Buddhas.
What are these four?"
One would rather lose body and life than slander the sutras and the Way;
throughout one's entire lifespan, one shall not revile bodhisattvas;
and even if harmed, one shall never associate with evil friends from the very beginning.
"Constantly recollecting all Buddhas and practicing the samādhi—
this constitutes the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I have never slandered the Buddha’s sutras or the Way, nor have I dared to speak ill of the Bodhisattvas’ shortcomings;
I have abandoned and distanced myself from evil associates, and I constantly keep the practices of all Buddhas in mind."

By practicing and studying this holy Dharma, one is thus able to meet with the Tathāgata and receive the acceptance of all the Most Victorious Ones, until finally attaining the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains the thirty-two marks. What are these four?"
They cut off their own precious treasures to provide for and distribute among the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata;
they blend various kinds of incense to create fragrant oil with which they anoint and fumigate them;
furthermore, they light lamps and scatter various flowers.
"To accord with and revere the noble ones, and to practice the Way and its teachings—
this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Rare and wondrous jewels offered to the Buddhist temples, Sumanā oil and incense burning as lamps,
Various kinds of flowers scattered as gifts— These noble and pleasing deeds do not lose their merit."
He attained the thirty-two extraordinary marks, upright and majestic, complete with all virtues;
through these dharmas he accomplished these marks, thereby becoming the most supreme Honored One among men.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can accomplish the eighty minor marks. What are these four?"
They constantly prepare various Dharma seats;
they serve others with humility and without weariness;
and they frequently go to visit and pay homage to Dharma teachers.
"To exhort and transform sentient beings so that they enter the Buddha-way—
this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Having spread various kinds of robes as seats, Serving others without ever growing weary,
And always longing for the Dharma for the sake of all beings— By these causes and conditions, one attains the eighty secondary marks."
Exhorting and transforming all sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s wisdom— if one practices this Dharma, there will be no difficulty on the path.
Once a bodhisattva has cultivated these merits, by means of them, they shall attain the eighty secondary marks.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains eloquence.
What are these four?"
They open the wondrous treasury of the Bodhisattvas to benefit and guide others; they recite and study the scriptures of the Buddhas of the three periods.
Day and night, they practice contemplation and remain awake in mindfulness three times each, such that all in the world place their trust in them.
They realize that the Way of the Buddhas neither arises nor ceases, and they maintain contentment while discerning and observing it with clarity.
"To be able to practice and uphold what has been taught without sparing one's body or life—
this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Carefully preserve and protect the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; day and night, practice the threefold Dharma.
Attaining the state of non-arising and being without greed for the world, one expounds and explains the teachings of all Buddhas.
Through joy and delight, one follows the transformative path and upholds the meaning of the Ten Powers as taught."
Never cherishing one's own body or life, one examines all conditioned phenomena for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.

Thus, one is able to practice these four virtues; by means of wondrous eloquence that accords with worldly conventions, one is honored and served by devas and humans, while wearing extraordinary ornaments and flower garlands.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains a buddha-field.
What are these four?"
They harbor no divergent thoughts;
their minds are always impartial;
they follow and accord with the Buddha-way.
"Not contradicting the fourfold assembly— this is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
Seeing others receive offerings, they never harbor jealousy toward them;
always practicing impartial compassion with a mind free of self, they remain detached from such honors, finding joy like that of space.
By means of these four immeasurable qualities, constantly protecting others while harboring a compassionate heart,
one attains a pure land of wondrous adornment and swiftly achieves the state of perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"A bodhisattva has four dharmas by which their retinue is always harmonious. What are these four?
He has never caused dissension among the families of others;
whenever there were disputes, he exhorted them toward reconciliation;
and he recited the sutras and the Dharma to instruct and guide people.
Furthermore, one abandons divisive speech and slander, and always speaks in praise of others.
This is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
Never having broken up the retinues of others, if there is strife, he exhorts them toward reconciliation;
reciting the Dharma and explaining it for others, he never from the start uses double-tongued speech to sow discord.
If one is able to practice these four dharmas, one will attain a retinue that is never dispersed;
because of this, the followers will be harmonious and pure, and by means of these four dharmas, all shall be fully accomplished.
The Buddha told Vimaladattā:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s aspiration for a buddha-field is fulfilled according to their wish.
What are these four?..."
If one sees others attain wisdom, one harbors no mind of jealousy;
one is constantly able to practice the six *pāramitās*;

and upon seeing various bodhisattvas—whether those who have first resolved their minds for enlightenment or those seated at the site of awakening—one regards them as Buddhas, making offerings and following them with an impartial mind, free from flattery or deceit.
"Without ever seeking after false virtues, one is nonetheless able to obtain the benefits of offerings.
This is the fourth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
Seeing virtue and making offerings without envy, aspiring with resolve to the pure pāramitās,
regarding all bodhisattvas as Buddhas, and harboring no flattery for the sake of gain or sustenance.
If a bodhisattva can cultivate these virtues, they will be able to reach and behold the Buddhas of the ten directions;
according to their wishes, they shall behold the Buddha-lands and immediately attain rebirth therein as they have conceived in their minds.
Thereupon, Vimaladattā addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"Regarding the instruction and admonition just provided by the World-Honored One, had I failed to uphold this Dharma and allowed it to be corrupted or leaked, I would have been in violation of and deceived the infinitely great sages, the Buddhas of the ten directions, who currently exist."
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Vimaladattā: "This matter is most wondrous; do not treat it lightly.

The Way and its Dharma are profound and subtle, which you have not yet fully understood. The practices of the bodhisattvas are also extremely difficult to accomplish; one cannot, in such a hasty manner, attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realize supreme perfect enlightenment while in a woman's body."
Vimaladattā, the daughter, replied to Maudgalyāyana:

"If what I have said is true and not false, then in a future age I shall attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and be named Buddha, the World-Honored One."

This trichiliocosm shook in six ways so that no sentient being would experience regression; the heavens rained down various flowers, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck. I transformed my female form to become a man, at the age of eight, when I first established this vow.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and lutes and musical instruments sounded of their own accord without being struck.
The girl Vimaladattā’s body transformed into the male form of an eight-year-old boy.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"O Heaven among Heavens!..."

From this day forward, I take refuge in all Bodhisattvas, as well as those who have first resolved their minds for enlightenment; I pay them homage, practicing humility and obedience to their teachings with utmost sincerity toward the Buddha-way. Why is this so?
Now this young woman is able to give rise to and manifest this Way, with transformations and majestic spiritual power that are infinite, sublime, and wondrous.
The sincere vows she has established shall all manifest as auspicious responses of the True Dharma; she shall fully achieve the fruition exactly as she has spoken.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Maudgalyāyana!
It is as you have said."

"From the first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment, through the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, until sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, one becomes a source of blessings for the multitudes of devas and the world, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

At that time, the Buddha smiled with joy. It is the law of all Buddhas that when they smile with joy, light of five colors issues from their mouths, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three in the upper realms; it then circles back three times and enters through the crown of the head. The Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, praising him in verse:
“His voice is like that of Great Brahmā, And like the sounds of devas, nāgas, and spirits;
It is like the mournful cry of a phoenix, Subtle, exquisite, most vast and elegant.”
The resonance is like the roar of thunder and rain, gladdening the hearts of all people.
Whenever you manifest a joyful smile, many leap for joy;
O Ocean of Great Virtue, by what cause do you, who possess the Ten Powers, smile?
I have explained this solely for the sake of analytical exposition, so that those who doubt may attain understanding.
The earth quaked in six ways, and there was no part of the land that did not shine;
soft flowers rained down, falling upon all the devas and humans.
You convert and restrain those of external heterodox paths, like a lion taming wild beasts.
I pray you will distinguish for me: for what reason do you smile with joy?
Even ten billion kotis of suns and moons, or the brilliance of bright pearls and the flames of lightning—
The gods, nāgas, and spirits, and the majesty and virtue of Brahmā,
King of Gods; when the Muni emits light, pure and free from dust and defilement,
it completely eclipses the brilliance of the ten directions, and only the Buddha’s light shines forth.
A white hair grows between his eyebrows, pure white like exquisite camphor;
fine and smooth as a fine garment, beautiful and lustrous like a pearl;
its holy radiance is like drifting clouds, illuminating hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands.
Venerated and looked up to by the multitude, I pray you tell me why you smile?
Your mind is perfectly composed; your brow-mark shows compassion for the world.
Subtle and surpassing the color of milk, it appears from afar like snow upon a mountain.
Blue, yellow, red, white, and black, Furthermore appearing like purple and crimson;
Countless thousands of rays of light Issue forth from the mouth of the Muni,
Illuminating the entirety of the three-thousandfold world system, Completely eclipsing the brilliance of the sun and moon.
Reaching even unto the void of space, it illuminates all sentient beings.
It can cause fire to be extinguished and water to dry up; even the great ocean may wither away.
Yet that which the Buddha has spoken with utmost sincerity has never been subject to variation.
Even if all the people of the ten directions were to become Pratyekabuddhas,
each endowed with supreme wisdom and a lifespan of a hundred billion *kṣepa* kalpas,
and were all to come before the Buddha at once to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma;
Simultaneously with the Benevolent One and others, a single voice resolves all doubts.
With the Infinite Perfection of Universal Wisdom, there is nothing he does not understand;
through his great merit and majesty, he alone proclaims the thirty-two extraordinary marks.
For what reason do you smile?
How do you explain the wisdom of the Path?
May the devas, the people of the world, and all beings hear your beautiful, gentle, and profound teaching.
The Buddha addressed the venerable Ānanda:

"Did you see Vimaladattā, who sought the path of the Buddha with resolve, established a vow of utmost sincerity, and—after the three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways—was transformed into a man?"
Ānanda said, “I see it. The Buddha said:

“Since the Bodhisattva Vigatarajas first resolved upon and practiced the path to unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment eighty hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, only then did Mañjuśrī resolve his mind on the Way.”
When that woman attains Buddhahood, furthermore, the pure buddha-fields of four hundred and eighty thousand bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī, shall constitute a single buddha-field.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked Vimaladattā:

"Noble son, you have established yourself in wisdom and have long since resolved upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; why then have you not yet transformed this female body?"
Vimala replied, “The World-Honored One has praised you, saying that your supernormal powers are most supreme.
For what reason do you not transform yourself into a man?”
Maudgalyāyana remained silent.
Vimaladattā said,
"One does not attain perfect enlightenment by means of a female body or a male form."
"Why is this? Because the Way has no arising, and there is nothing that can achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“It is difficult to fathom, World-Honored One!
The Bodhisattva Vimaladatta has entered so deeply into the subtle and wondrous that his majesty is truly such as this.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“The Bodhisattva Vimaladatta practiced the samādhi of emptiness under sixty billion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
he received and practiced the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) under eighty billion Buddhas;
and he inquired about the profound and subtle chapters on the bodhisattva path under thirty billion Buddhas.”
He made offerings and served eighty billion Buddhas with food, delicacies, clothing, and alms bowls.
This was his ultimate practice, which he had resolved upon without doubt; desiring to achieve full realization and to transform all beings, he asked about the Seal Samādhi.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive this sutra-dharma and extensively expound it for others with detailed analysis, their merit shall be immeasurable."

Suppose there were someone who filled as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with the seven treasures and offered them in alms; this would not equal the merit of receiving, upholding, and reciting this sutra, for that merit exceeds the former beyond measure.
"These bodhisattvas, by virtue of the law of karmic retribution, require food and drink; from this they shall attain accomplishment.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha, "What is the name of this sutra?"
"How should one practice and uphold it?
The Buddha said, "This sutra is titled 'The Questions of Vimaladatta on the Universal Attainment of Discriminative Eloquence'; you should receive and uphold it."
While this sutra was being spoken, eight billion devas and humans reached the ultimate, definitive resolution regarding the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānasañcaya addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“How long will it be before the Bodhisattva Vimaladatta shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment and become a Most Perfect Buddha?”
The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!

After passing through hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you shall attain the Way of the Buddha. You shall be named King of Undefiled Radiant Glory (Vimalaprabhāśrīrāja) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. The kalpa shall be named Infinite Virtue and Freedom; it shall be the dwelling place for śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, where their clothing, food, and drink will be just like those in the heavens."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladatta, having heard the Buddha bestow his prediction of enlightenment, leaped into the air to a height of eight hundred and seven *li* above the ground. He emitted a radiance from his body that illuminated hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands. Above the World-Honored One, he manifested eighty-four thousand canopies made of exquisite jewels as an offering to the Buddha. Then, within the void, he displayed countless miraculous transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and paid homage to the Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, throughout the ten directions, who were beyond measure or calculation.
Having completed their offerings, they immediately returned and stood before the Buddha.

At that time, the Brahmā, the brahmin, and the assembly of five hundred, having heard the Buddha bestow the prophecy of certainty upon Vimaladattā and having witnessed the benefits of his miraculous transformations, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. A sense of self-congratulation arose within them, and with one accord, they uttered these verses in praise:
“For those who revere and honor the Buddha, Such great and beneficial merit shall arise.”
If one bows one's head to the Perfectly Awakened One, one immediately attains the Dharma of equality.
Having committed offenses and transgressions in past lives, he was born into the family of a brahmin;
upon seeing a disciple of the World-Honored One, he proclaimed with his own mouth that it was an ill omen.
Now I alone repent of my transgression; because I sat and spoke these words, I beheld the sons of the Buddhas whose speech did not accord with the truth.
I failed to see the World-Honored One, the Sovereign King among men.
To have attained a human body would be of no benefit, nor should one accept food and drink.
Vimaladatta, know this: our offerings were in vain;
having beheld the sons of the Buddha, we prostrate ourselves in reverence.
Please speak for our sake: when I was first born and fell to the ground, I beheld the Teacher and immediately heard the name of the Buddha.
He extolled the noble virtues that are upright, true, and without falsehood.
We all, having heard this, aspire to the Way. This is due to the remaining merit from our past lives, that we have again been able to hear the Buddha’s voice;
having come to the presence of the Teacher, we listen to and contemplate the meaning of the scriptures.
Having seen and paid homage to the World-Honored One, and having heard and examined the unsurpassed Dharma,
because of encountering the Teacher, one is liberated from all suffering and affliction.
The Protector of the World brings great peace by means of preaching this Dharma.
We shall study this, for through it all Buddha-dharmas are accomplished;
hearing and practicing the True Path, we shall bring about all Buddha-dharmas.
Out of compassion for us, you have proclaimed the practice of the True Reality.
He preached the gateway of the Way, that which a bodhisattva should uphold;
it is the practice of equality, which brings about the illumination of the world’s path.
Having seen such a state of mind, the Buddha immediately smiled with joy.
Ānanda asked the World-Honored One:
"O Supreme among Men, please explain:
as for these five hundred brahmins standing here before us,"
They shall all, in one and the same eon, attain the state of the Buddha, the Guide.
Having already undergone this in previous lives by making offerings to five hundred Buddhas,
once their lifespans here have ended, they shall behold billions of Buddhas.
Throughout eighty billion kalpas, you shall never fall into the evil realms;
in each and every kalpa, you shall behold billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
Following these distinct kalpas, you shall become a Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
They shall be known by the name Brahmans; they will all share the same eon, their lifespans being entirely equal at eighty billion eons each.
Their noble lands and holy assemblies will be identical, with eighty billion bhikṣus in each.
"Guiding and benefiting all living beings, transforming and enlightening hundreds of millions of people;
wherever they gradually dwell and reside, they remain tranquil and free from attachment.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

Vimaladattā, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, five hundred brahmans and brahmins, King Prasenajit, the community of bhikṣus, devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, and human beings, having heard the sutra, rejoiced, paid homage, and departed.
